title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
keywords: saints are sinners who keep trying
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's address to the Calamba City Lawyers League (August 24, 2001), applying to lawyers his three personal cornerstones, the '3 E-values': excellence, ethics and eternity (earlier expounded in his book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity')

The premise that the legal profession is akin to a religious vocation ('many are called, but few are chosen'), set against the low public esteem for lawyers (Dennis Prager's claim that law school teaches 'Is it legal?' rather than 'Is it right?'; Salonga's lament that no lawyer has been president since Marcos)

Excellence as more than competence -- taking responsibility, sincerity, and serving the underprivileged and oppressed rather than chasing power, wealth or acclaim, guided by the Code of Professional Responsibility

Ethics as fidelity to a threefold hierarchy of responsibilities (justice first, the client second, the lawyer's self last) flowing from integrity and moral courage; and eternity -- belief in life after death with God at the center -- as the value that transforms one's whole value system, so a lawyer can be 'holy in a not-so-holy profession'
sub_topics: The occasion: inducting Atty. Emilio C. Capulong Jr. (a leading light of Bantay Katarungan and Kilosbayan) as new league president; Capulong equates being a lawyer with being a servant of the Lord, the inspiration for the address

The vocation parallel: law, like the clergy, demands 'patience, perseverance and prayer'; both pass through rigorous training, sacrifice and soul-searching -- yet lawyers are not 'an admired, adored or adulated lot'

The critique of the profession: Dennis Prager ('Happiness Is A Serious Problem') argues law school can make people worse by teaching them to ask 'Is it legal?' rather than 'Is it right?'; former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga notes 'widespread cynicism about lawyers' and that no lawyer has been chosen president since Ferdinand Marcos

Excellence (the first E): more than knowledge, procedure and courtroom skill -- it involves taking responsibility, sincerity and making a difference; success requires mind, heart and soul at peace, not short-lived gains

Excellence as devotion to work and altruism: against pursuing law only for honor, prestige and money (which breeds the 'rotten few'); the Code of Professional Responsibility forbids dishonest or deceitful conduct and requires upholding the integrity and dignity of the profession and serving the defenseless

Ethics (the second E): the threefold hierarchy of a lawyer's responsibilities -- first, as officers of the court, the interest of justice; second, the client's cause; third (farthest), the lawyer's personal interest; CJP rues that some have inverted it (self first, client next, justice last)

Clarifying that the Supreme Court 'has not issued any circular or memorandum reversing the lawyer's hierarchy of responsibilities'; ethics proceeds from integrity, which is moral courage -- 'only one who is clear of mind and pure of heart can act with integrity'

The innate moral compass: humans are 'inherently possessed of a general discernment of what is good and what is bad,' so maintaining ethics, if we stay true to being creatures of a good God, 'would entail no effort at all'

Eternity (the third E): belief that life on earth is not the only one -- there is life after death; just as there are human and physical laws, there are spiritual laws with penalties for transgressing God's commands; placing God at the center is the key to understanding what is true and just

The epilogue: lawyers can be 'on a level with any other pontificate' through excellence, ethics and eternity; 'if there is truth to the aphorism that saints are sinners who keep trying,' then 'let us begin our journey to sainthood' -- being 'holy in a not-so-holy profession'

stances.claim: The legal profession can be a calling as noble as the religious vocation, but only if lawyers reject the cynicism that asks 'Is it legal?' instead of 'Is it right?'; lawyers must serve the underprivileged and the cause of justice rather than chase 'power, wealth or acclaim,' for 'short-lived gains in this earthly existence cannot compare with the rewards that await us yonder.'
stances.rhetorical_move: law-as-vocation parallel: elevating lawyering to a quasi-priestly calling to shame the profit-and-prestige motive and recover an altruistic ideal
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's governing ideal for the profession

stances.claim: Every lawyer owes a fixed hierarchy of responsibilities -- the interest of justice first (as officers of the court), the client's cause a 'far second,' and the lawyer's personal interest a 'farther third'; some have inverted this order (self first, justice last), but the Supreme Court 'has not issued any circular reversing' it. Ethics proceeds from integrity, which is moral courage, and 'only one who is clear of mind and pure of heart can act with integrity.'
stances.rhetorical_move: hierarchy-of-responsibilities ordering, reinforced by an authoritative denial that the order has changed, to rebuke lawyers who put self before justice

stances.claim: The acceptance of eternity -- life after death, spiritual laws, and God at the center -- 'will dramatically transform our entire value system'; placing God at the center is what lets a lawyer 'truly achieve a complete understanding of what is true and just,' so that one can be 'holy in a not-so-holy profession.'
stances.rhetorical_move: eternity-as-value-transformer: grounding professional ethics in a transcendent, faith-based horizon rather than in secular rules alone
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's personal and spiritual conviction

notable_anecdotes: The 'Is it legal?' indictment: CJP cites Dennis Prager's 'Happiness Is A Serious Problem' -- that many people 'are worse human beings' after law school because it teaches them to ask 'Is it legal?' rather than 'Is it right?' -- as the cynic's case against the profession he means to rebut.

Salonga's barometer: he quotes Jovito Salonga's observation that whereas before martial law most Philippine presidents were lawyers, 'no lawyer has been chosen president since Ferdinand Marcos' -- a measure of how far public esteem for lawyers has fallen.

The inverted hierarchy: CJP says he has encountered lawyers who understood the order of duties 'the other way around' -- their own interest first, the client's next, and justice last, if at all -- and pointedly notes the Court has issued no circular reversing the proper hierarchy.

Capulong as living text: the address is inspired by inductee Atty. Emilio Capulong Jr., who 'equates his being a lawyer to his being a servant of the Lord,' embodying the dual loyalty to the law of humans and the commandments of God that CJP holds up as the model.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's August 24, 2001 address to the Calamba City Lawyers League, inducting Atty. Emilio C. Capulong Jr. -- a Bantay Katarungan and Kilosbayan figure who 'equates being a lawyer with being a servant of the Lord.' CJP develops the parallel between law and the religious vocation ('many are called, but few are chosen'), confronting the low public esteem for lawyers -- Dennis Prager's charge that law school teaches students to ask 'Is it legal?' rather than 'Is it right?,' and Jovito Salonga's lament that no lawyer has been president since Marcos. Against this, he offers his three personal cornerstones, the '3 E-values.' Excellence is more than competence; it is responsibility, sincerity and 'making a difference,' pursued not for 'power, wealth or acclaim' but in service of the underprivileged, as the Code of Professional Responsibility requires. Ethics is fidelity to a threefold hierarchy of responsibilities -- the interest of justice first (lawyers are officers of the court), the client's cause a 'far second,' and the lawyer's personal interest a 'farther third' -- a hierarchy some have inverted but which, he stresses, the Supreme Court has issued no circular to reverse; ethics flows from integrity, which is moral courage, and 'only one who is clear of mind and pure of heart can act with integrity.' Eternity, the third E, is the belief that life on earth is not all there is: just as there are human and physical laws, there are spiritual laws, and placing God at the center transforms one's entire value system and reveals 'what is true and just.' He closes that lawyers can stand 'on a level with any other pontificate' through excellence, ethics and eternity -- and that 'if there is truth to the aphorism that saints are sinners who keep trying,' then 'let us begin our journey to sainthood,' becoming 'holy in a not-so-holy profession.'
